subjective.vernacular: Do you get headaches, and if so, where and when do they happen?
subjective.why_it_matters: Occipital morning headaches can signal poorly controlled or secondary hypertension, while absence of headache is the norm in primary hypertension.

subjective.term: Family history of hypertension or cardiovascular disease
subjective.vernacular: Do close blood relatives have high blood pressure, heart attacks, or strokes?
subjective.why_it_matters: Strong family history increases prior probability of essential hypertension and helps stratify overall cardiovascular risk.

subjective.vernacular: How often do you eat processed, canned, or restaurant foods, or add salt at the table?
subjective.why_it_matters: High sodium intake is a modifiable driver of salt-sensitive essential hypertension and can be targeted without medication.

subjective.vernacular: How many alcoholic drinks do you have in a typical week?
subjective.why_it_matters: Regular alcohol use above 2 drinks/day is an independent, reversible cause of elevated blood pressure.

subjective.vernacular: Do you snore loudly, stop breathing during sleep, or wake up feeling unrefreshed?
subjective.why_it_matters: Obstructive sleep apnea is one of the most common secondary causes of hypertension and is often undiagnosed.

subjective.vernacular: Are you taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or supplements — especially NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, or oral contraceptives?
subjective.why_it_matters: Many common medications raise blood pressure and represent a fully reversible secondary cause.

subjective.vernacular: Do you ever have sudden spells of pounding heartbeat, severe headache, sweating, and anxiety all at once?
subjective.why_it_matters: These classic paroxysmal spells raise suspicion for pheochromocytoma, a rare but life-threatening secondary cause.

subjective.vernacular: How many days per week do you get at least 30 minutes of moderate exercise?
subjective.why_it_matters: Physical inactivity is an independent risk factor for essential hypertension and cardiovascular disease.

subjective.vernacular: Have you noticed drinking much more water than usual or urinating much more frequently?
subjective.why_it_matters: Excessive thirst and urination can signal primary hyperaldosteronism (causing hypokalemia) or undiagnosed diabetes, both of which can drive hypertension.

subjective.vernacular: Have you gained significant weight over the past few years, and where do you carry it?
subjective.why_it_matters: Central obesity is strongly linked to metabolic syndrome and essential hypertension, while rapid weight gain with other features may suggest Cushing syndrome.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever had kidney stones, blood in your urine, or repeated kidney infections?
subjective.why_it_matters: Prior kidney disease or recurrent infections raise the probability of renovascular or renal parenchymal hypertension.

subjective.vernacular: Do you smoke or use tobacco products, and if you used to, when did you stop?
subjective.why_it_matters: Smoking amplifies cardiovascular risk substantially and influences the urgency and target of blood pressure management.

objective.term: Carotid or abdominal bruit on auscultation
objective.vernacular: Listening with a stethoscope over the neck arteries and the belly to detect turbulent blood flow suggesting arterial narrowing

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure with no single identifiable cause — the most common type, shaped by genetics, lifestyle, and aging
not_yet_testable: o-006 (basic metabolic panel — not yet ordered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Essential hypertension accounts for approximately 90–95% of all hypertension cases in adults; prior probability dominates at presentation.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No record data yet; estimate based on population prevalence only.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated for years, this silently damages the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes — raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, and kidney failure.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure caused or worsened by repeated breathing interruptions during sleep
not_yet_testable: s-005 (sleep-disordered breathing symptoms — not yet gathered)
s-010 (weight and obesity — not yet gathered)
assessment_candidates.basis: OSA is present in up to 30–40% of hypertensive patients and is the most prevalent identifiable secondary cause; hypertension from OSA is often resistant to standard treatment.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot assess without sleep history and anthropometric data; estimate is a conservative prior.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If undiagnosed, OSA-driven hypertension resists medication and continues to stress the heart and brain around the clock.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: The adrenal glands produce too much of a salt-retaining hormone, raising blood pressure and lowering potassium
assessment_candidates.basis: Primary hyperaldosteronism is now recognized in roughly 5–10% of hypertensive patients, making it the most common endocrine secondary cause; it is curable or controllable with targeted therapy.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No biochemical data yet; estimate based on published prevalence in hypertensive populations.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Missed primary hyperaldosteronism leads to excess cardiovascular events beyond what blood pressure alone would predict, and a potentially curable cause goes untreated.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Blood pressure raised by a drug or supplement the person is taking — such as NSAIDs, stimulants, decongestants, or hormonal contraceptives
not_yet_testable: s-006 (medication and supplement use — not yet gathered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Numerous common medications elevate blood pressure through well-characterized mechanisms; identifying and stopping the offending agent can resolve hypertension without additional drugs.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Entirely untestable until a complete medication list is obtained.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Continued use of the causative medication negates any treatment and unnecessarily exposes the person to cardiovascular risk.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Narrowing of the arteries supplying one or both kidneys tricks the body into thinking blood pressure is too low, driving it much higher
assessment_candidates.basis: Renovascular hypertension accounts for 1–5% of all hypertension; it should be considered especially in young women (fibromuscular dysplasia) or older patients with diffuse atherosclerosis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Age and sex are unknown; estimate is a conservative prevalence-based prior.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated renovascular hypertension can cause progressive kidney loss and is resistant to standard blood pressure medications.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: An overactive or underactive thyroid gland disrupting blood pressure regulation
assessment_candidates.basis: Both hypothyroidism (raising diastolic pressure) and hyperthyroidism (raising systolic pressure) are well-recognized secondary causes of hypertension, and both are readily treated.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No thyroid history or lab data available; estimate reflects general population prevalence of thyroid disease.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Treating the thyroid disorder typically normalizes or substantially improves blood pressure without adding antihypertensive drugs.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A rare tumor of the adrenal gland that releases surges of adrenaline-like hormones, causing dangerous spikes in blood pressure
not_yet_testable: o-006 (basic metabolic panel — not yet ordered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Pheochromocytoma is rare (prevalence ~0.1–0.6% of hypertensive patients) but must remain on the list because missing it is life-threatening; surgical cure is possible.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Very low prior probability, but severity mandates inclusion; paroxysmal symptom history will significantly shift this estimate.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: A missed pheochromocytoma can trigger a hypertensive crisis causing stroke, heart attack, or sudden death — particularly during surgery or with certain medications.

residual.vernacular: Something not on this list — the differential is never closed

plan_options.vernacular: Structured guidance on reducing salt, increasing physical activity, moderating alcohol, and reaching a healthier weight
plan_options.basis: ACC/AHA 2017 Hypertension Guidelines recommend lifestyle modification as first-line treatment for stage 1 hypertension, capable of reducing systolic BP by 4–11 mmHg.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician, registered dietitian, or certified health coach

plan_options.vernacular: A portable device worn for 24 hours to record blood pressure throughout the day and night, ruling out white-coat effect
plan_options.basis: ABPM is the reference standard for confirming true hypertension and ruling out white-coat hypertension before committing to lifelong treatment.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician

plan_options.vernacular: Starting a blood pressure–lowering medication if lifestyle changes alone are insufficient or cardiovascular risk is elevated
plan_options.basis: ACC/AHA guidelines support pharmacotherapy for stage 1 hypertension when 10-year ASCVD risk is ≥10% or when BP remains ≥130/80 after lifestyle intervention.
plan_options.who_can_act: Licensed prescriber (physician, NP, PA)

plan_options.term: Polysomnography or home sleep apnea test
plan_options.vernacular: An overnight sleep study to measure breathing pauses, oxygen dips, and sleep quality
plan_options.basis: AHA/ASA and ACC guidelines recommend evaluation for OSA in resistant or difficult-to-control hypertension; treating OSA with CPAP reduces BP by a meaningful amount.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician (referral) or sleep medicine specialist

plan_options.vernacular: A blood test taken under standardized conditions to screen for overactive adrenal hormone production
plan_options.basis: The Endocrine Society recommends ARR screening in all patients with hypertension and unprovoked hypokalemia, or in those under age 40 with stage 1 hypertension.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician or endocrinologist

plan_options.vernacular: A urine collection over a full day to detect breakdown products of adrenaline-like hormones released by a tumor
plan_options.basis: Endocrine Society guidelines recommend biochemical testing for pheochromocytoma when episodic symptoms or resistant hypertension are present; urine fractionated metanephrines have >95% sensitivity.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician or endocrinologist

plan_options.vernacular: Using age, sex, cholesterol, blood pressure, and smoking status to estimate the chance of a heart attack or stroke in the next 10 years
plan_options.basis: ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations are the standard tool to guide treatment intensity decisions in stage 1 hypertension.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician (requires lipid panel and complete history)

subjective.why_it_matters: First-degree family history strongly supports essential hypertension and elevates lifetime cardiovascular risk.

subjective.vernacular: How often do you exercise or do physical activity each week?

subjective.why_it_matters: Major weight loss reduces blood pressure; GLP-1 agonists can lower BP independent of weight and alter cardiovascular risk.

subjective.vernacular: Do you have muscle cramps, weakness, or urinate much more than usual?
subjective.why_it_matters: Hypokalemia with hypertension raises concern for primary aldosteronism, the most common secondary cause.

subjective.vernacular: Do you smoke cigarettes, use chewing tobacco, or vape now or in the past?
subjective.why_it_matters: Tobacco use amplifies cardiovascular risk in hypertension and acutely raises blood pressure.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure with no single identifiable cause — the most common type, driven by genetics, diet, and lifestyle
assessment_candidates.basis: Accounts for ~90–95% of hypertension; family history of essential HTN, high dietary sodium, and stage 1 BP reading are all consistent.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Most probable category but cannot be confirmed until secondary causes are reasonably excluded.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated essential hypertension over years substantially raises lifetime risk of stroke, heart attack, heart failure, and kidney failure.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure driven by repeated oxygen drops during sleep, which keep the nervous system in a high-alert state
not_yet_testable: o-011 (CPAP compliance data — not yet reviewed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Severe OSA is a well-established secondary cause of hypertension; prevalence of OSA-related HTN is 30–50% in OSA patients. CPAP adequacy unknown.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: High clinical plausibility given confirmed severe OSA, but whether CPAP is controlling it is unknown — residual AHI data are essential.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If OSA is the primary driver and goes untreated, blood pressure will remain elevated and cardiovascular risk stays high despite any medication.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure caused by insufficient thyroid hormone, which raises vascular resistance — worsened if levothyroxine dose is too low
assessment_candidates.basis: Hypothyroidism raises diastolic BP through increased systemic vascular resistance; inadequate levothyroxine replacement is a correctable cause.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot assess without current TSH; levothyroxine use indicates pre-existing thyroid disease making this a real possibility.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If undertreated hypothyroidism is driving BP elevation, dose adjustment alone could normalize or substantially improve blood pressure.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: An adrenal gland tumor or overgrowth that makes too much aldosterone hormone, causing salt retention and high blood pressure
assessment_candidates.basis: Most common secondary cause of hypertension (~5–10% of all HTN cases); absence of muscle cramps reduces but does not exclude it — normokalemic aldosteronism is common.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Absence of hypokalemia symptoms is mildly reassuring but does not rule out; screening ARR is recommended in unexplained stage 1–2 HTN.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Undiagnosed primary aldosteronism carries disproportionately high risk of cardiac and renal damage beyond that explained by blood pressure level alone.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Narrowing of the arteries supplying the kidneys, causing the kidneys to send signals that raise blood pressure
assessment_candidates.basis: Accounts for 1–5% of hypertension; more likely in younger patients, women with fibromuscular dysplasia, or older patients with diffuse atherosclerosis.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No smoking history and no stimulant use slightly lowers atherosclerosis risk, but cannot exclude without physical exam and labs.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Unrecognized renal artery stenosis can cause accelerated kidney failure and resistant hypertension that does not respond to standard medications.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A rare adrenal tumor that releases adrenaline surges, causing episodes of very high blood pressure, sweating, and heart pounding
assessment_candidates.basis: Rare (<0.5% of HTN) but life-threatening if missed; absence of paroxysmal symptoms substantially lowers probability.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Paroxysmal symptom denial makes this unlikely, but it remains on the list due to severity and occasional silent presentation.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Undiagnosed pheochromocytoma can cause hypertensive crisis, stroke, or cardiac arrest — potentially fatal.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Blood pressure that reads high only in a medical setting due to anxiety, but is normal at home or on ambulatory monitoring
not_yet_testable: o-001 (only single reading obtained — repeat and home readings needed)
assessment_candidates.basis: Prevalence ~15–30% of patients with apparent stage 1 HTN in clinic; single clinic reading without home or ambulatory confirmation cannot exclude this.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Cannot confirm or exclude without home blood pressure monitoring or ambulatory 24-hour recording — single reading of 150/90 is insufficient.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If white-coat hypertension is the explanation, unnecessary antihypertensive treatment could cause harmful blood pressure drops.

plan_options.term: Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) — confirm diagnosis
plan_options.vernacular: Take blood pressure twice daily for 1–2 weeks at home with a validated cuff to confirm readings are truly elevated outside the clinic
plan_options.basis: AHA/ACC 2017 guidelines recommend out-of-office BP confirmation before initiating treatment for stage 1 hypertension.
plan_options.who_can_act: Patient (self-monitored with validated device); reviewed by clinician

plan_options.vernacular: Reduce added salt and processed food sodium to under 2,300 mg per day — this alone can lower blood pressure 5–6 mmHg
plan_options.basis: DASH diet and sodium restriction are first-line lifestyle interventions with Level A evidence for stage 1 HTN.
plan_options.who_can_act: Clinician, dietitian, or patient self-directed

plan_options.vernacular: Download data from the CPAP machine to check how many hours per night it is used and how many breathing pauses remain
plan_options.basis: Effective CPAP therapy (AHI < 5/hr, ≥4 hrs/night use) reduces systolic BP 2–10 mmHg in OSA; uncontrolled OSA is a reversible BP contributor.
plan_options.who_can_act: Sleep medicine clinician or primary care provider with access to device download

plan_options.vernacular: Blood test to check whether the thyroid hormone replacement dose is correct
plan_options.basis: AHA recommends checking TSH in hypertensive patients on thyroid replacement to exclude undertreated hypothyroidism as a cause.
plan_options.who_can_act: Clinician (order); patient (blood draw)

plan_options.term: Basic metabolic panel, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, lipid panel
plan_options.vernacular: Blood and urine tests to check kidney function, electrolytes, blood sugar, and cholesterol — required before starting any BP medication
plan_options.basis: AHA/ACC 2017 guidelines list these as standard initial workup for newly diagnosed hypertension.
plan_options.who_can_act: Clinician (order); patient (blood draw and urine sample)

plan_options.vernacular: Heart tracing to check for thickening of the heart muscle (left ventricular hypertrophy) caused by years of high blood pressure
plan_options.basis: LVH on ECG identifies end-organ damage, reclassifies risk, and may accelerate treatment decision per ACC/AHA guidelines.
plan_options.who_can_act: Clinician (order); performed by medical staff

plan_options.vernacular: Blood test to screen for an adrenal hormone imbalance — recommended if initial workup shows low potassium or BP proves hard to control
plan_options.basis: Endocrine Society guidelines recommend ARR screening in all patients with hypertension and spontaneous hypokalemia, or stage 2 HTN — reasonable to obtain at baseline.
plan_options.who_can_act: Clinician (order); patient (blood draw, morning, seated)

plan_options.term: Initiation of antihypertensive pharmacotherapy if lifestyle measures insufficient
plan_options.vernacular: Start a blood pressure–lowering medication (commonly a thiazide diuretic, ACE inhibitor, ARB, or calcium channel blocker) if home readings confirm stage 1 HTN and 10-year cardiovascular risk is ≥10%
plan_options.basis: AHA/ACC 2017 guidelines recommend drug therapy for stage 1 HTN when 10-year ASCVD risk ≥10% or if stage 2 (≥140/90 confirmed).
plan_options.who_can_act: Licensed clinician (prescriber)

plan_options.vernacular: A calculation using age, sex, cholesterol, blood pressure, and other factors to estimate the 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke — guides how aggressively to treat
plan_options.basis: Required per AHA/ACC 2017 guidelines to determine treatment threshold in stage 1 hypertension.
plan_options.who_can_act: Clinician (requires lipid panel results)

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure with no single identifiable cause — the most common type, driven by genetics, diet, and lifestyle

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Too much thyroid hormone from thyroid medication raising blood pressure and heart rate

assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If corrected, blood pressure and heart rate normalize without need for antihypertensive drugs — a fixable cause.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: An adrenal gland producing too much aldosterone hormone, causing sodium retention and high blood pressure
assessment_candidates.basis: Primary aldosteronism accounts for ~10% of all hypertension and up to 20% of resistant cases; often normokalemic; no paroxysmal symptoms or muscle weakness reported but potassium not measured.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Absence of weakness or cramps lowers probability but normokalemic primary aldosteronism is well-documented; requires ARR to exclude.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated primary aldosteronism causes disproportionate cardiovascular damage relative to BP level alone and is potentially surgically curable.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: Narrowing of the arteries feeding the kidneys triggers a hormonal cascade that raises blood pressure
not_yet_testable: o-013 (renal artery imaging — not yet ordered)
assessment_candidates.basis: Accounts for ~1–5% of hypertension; more likely in younger patients, those with early-onset resistant HTN, or atherosclerotic risk burden; no strong features here.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No strong clinical predictors present; low but non-negligible prior especially if creatinine is elevated or BP proves resistant to treatment.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Unrecognized renal artery stenosis leads to progressive kidney loss and refractory hypertension — treatable if caught early.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: A rare adrenal tumor that releases surges of adrenaline, causing dangerous spikes in blood pressure
assessment_candidates.basis: Prevalence ~0.1–0.6% of hypertensive patients; classic triad absent; still warrants mention given severity class and the fact that it is missed without testing.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Very unlikely given absent paroxysmal symptoms, but severity mandates it remain on the list until biochemical screening is done if BP is resistant.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Missed pheochromocytoma can cause fatal hypertensive crisis during surgery or stress — the stakes of missing it are catastrophic.

residual.vernacular: Something not on this list — the differential is never closed

plan_options.term: Repeat blood pressure measurement — bilateral, two occasions
plan_options.vernacular: Confirm high blood pressure with readings on at least two separate visits or with home monitoring over 1–2 weeks
plan_options.basis: ACC/AHA 2017 guideline: diagnosis requires average of ≥2 readings on ≥2 occasions; white-coat effect is common.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician or nurse; patient can self-monitor with validated home device

plan_options.vernacular: Reduce added salt and processed food to bring daily sodium below 2,300 mg — can lower blood pressure by 5–6 mmHg
plan_options.basis: DASH trial and ACC/AHA 2017 guideline: sodium restriction is a first-line lifestyle intervention for hypertension.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician, dietitian, or nurse educator

plan_options.vernacular: Check CPAP usage data to confirm the machine is being used correctly and controlling sleep apnea — if not, blood pressure may not improve
plan_options.basis: Meta-analyses show effective CPAP reduces systolic BP by 2–3 mmHg; inadequate use negates benefit.
plan_options.who_can_act: Sleep medicine specialist or CPAP equipment provider; primary care clinician can initiate referral

plan_options.vernacular: Blood test to confirm thyroid hormone replacement is at the right dose and not too high
plan_options.basis: ATA guideline: TSH should be checked at least annually in patients on levothyroxine; over-replacement is a correctable cause of hypertension.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician or endocrinologist

plan_options.term: Basic metabolic panel, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid panel, urine ACR
plan_options.vernacular: Standard blood and urine tests to check kidneys, electrolytes, cholesterol, and diabetes — all needed before starting blood pressure medication
plan_options.basis: ACC/AHA 2017 and JNC 8 guidelines: baseline labs required before initiating antihypertensive therapy to guide drug selection and detect target-organ damage.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician

plan_options.term: Serum potassium and aldosterone-to-renin ratio screening
plan_options.vernacular: Blood tests to check for a hormone imbalance from the adrenal gland that may be driving blood pressure up
plan_options.basis: Endocrine Society 2016 guideline recommends ARR screening in all stage 2 hypertension, resistant hypertension, or spontaneous hypokalemia.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician; confirmatory testing by endocrinologist

plan_options.vernacular: Heart tracing to check whether the heart muscle has thickened from pumping against high pressure — changes treatment urgency
plan_options.basis: ACC/AHA 2017 guideline: ECG is recommended as part of initial hypertension workup to detect LVH and arrhythmia.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician or cardiologist

plan_options.term: Initiate antihypertensive pharmacotherapy — thiazide, ACE inhibitor/ARB, or CCB
plan_options.vernacular: Start a blood pressure medication if lifestyle changes alone are insufficient — choice depends on lab results, kidney function, and other conditions
plan_options.basis: ACC/AHA 2017: drug therapy indicated for stage 1 HTN (≥130/80) with 10-year ASCVD risk ≥10%, or for any stage 2 HTN (≥140/90); BP here is 150/90.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician or cardiologist — requires prescription

subjective.vernacular: Do you get headaches, especially in the back of your head in the morning?
subjective.why_it_matters: Occipital headache can indicate elevated intracranial pressure from severe hypertension, helping gauge symptom burden and urgency.

subjective.vernacular: Has anyone in your immediate family (parents, siblings) been told they have high blood pressure?
subjective.why_it_matters: First-degree family history of hypertension strongly supports essential (primary) hypertension as the underlying cause.

subjective.vernacular: Do you add salt to your food or eat a lot of processed or salty foods?
subjective.why_it_matters: High sodium intake is a modifiable driver of primary hypertension and directly relevant to lifestyle modification planning.

subjective.vernacular: How much alcohol do you drink in a typical week?
subjective.why_it_matters: Alcohol intake above 2 drinks/day raises blood pressure and is a reversible secondary cause to exclude.
subjective.value: Less than one beer per week — minimal alcohol intake.

subjective.term: Obstructive sleep apnea — symptoms and treatment
subjective.vernacular: Do you snore loudly or stop breathing during sleep? Have you ever had a sleep study?
subjective.why_it_matters: OSA is the most common identifiable secondary cause of resistant hypertension; confirmed OSA with CPAP use is directly relevant to BP management.
subjective.value: Loud snoring, severe OSA diagnosed by sleep study, uses CPAP machine.

subjective.term: Current medication use including OTC and pressor agents
subjective.vernacular: What medications, vitamins, or supplements are you currently taking, including over-the-counter drugs like ibuprofen or nasal decongestants?
subjective.why_it_matters: NSAIDs (ibuprofen noted in record), decongestants, stimulants, and oral contraceptives can all raise blood pressure and represent reversible secondary causes.
subjective.value: Takes Synthroid (thyroid replacement); ibuprofen noted in shared care plan record.
subjective.missing: Frequency, dose, and indication for ibuprofen use not confirmed; OCP/hormonal contraceptive use not addressed given PCOS diagnosis.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever used cocaine, amphetamines, or other stimulant drugs?
subjective.why_it_matters: Stimulant substances cause acute and chronic BP elevation and must be excluded as a secondary contributor.

subjective.vernacular: How often do you exercise or do physical activity in a typical week?
subjective.why_it_matters: Physical inactivity contributes to primary hypertension and is a key target for lifestyle modification.

subjective.term: Chest pain or dyspnea — hypertensive target organ symptoms
subjective.vernacular: Have you had chest pain, chest tightness, or shortness of breath recently?
subjective.why_it_matters: Cardiac symptoms alongside BP of 195/194 mmHg raise concern for hypertensive emergency with end-organ involvement.
subjective.value: No chest pain or dyspnea reported.

subjective.term: Recent weight change and GLP-1 agonist use
subjective.vernacular: Have you recently lost or gained significant weight, and are you taking any weight-loss medications?
subjective.why_it_matters: Significant weight loss (50 lbs on GLP-1) can lower blood pressure, making the persistent hypertension more notable, and GLP-1 agents have mild antihypertensive effects.

subjective.vernacular: Do you ever get sudden attacks of headache, pounding heart, sweating, and very high blood pressure all at once?
subjective.why_it_matters: Classic triad of episodic headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis with severe BP spikes suggests pheochromocytoma as a secondary cause.

subjective.vernacular: Have you ever smoked cigarettes or used other tobacco or nicotine products?
subjective.why_it_matters: Smoking is a major cardiovascular risk factor that compounds hypertension-related end-organ risk.

subjective.vernacular: Have you noticed any blurring, double vision, or changes in your eyesight recently?
subjective.why_it_matters: Visual symptoms in the setting of severe BP elevation suggest possible hypertensive retinopathy or cerebral involvement requiring urgent evaluation.

subjective.vernacular: Are you using your CPAP machine every night, and do you feel rested when you wake up?
subjective.why_it_matters: Inadequate CPAP use leaves OSA-driven sympathetic activation uncontrolled, sustaining elevated blood pressure despite treatment.
subjective.missing: CPAP adherence and residual AHI on therapy not yet established.

objective.term: Blood pressure — most recent clinic reading
objective.vernacular: Blood pressure measured in the office or clinic.
objective.value: 150/90 mmHg (patient-entered 2026-07-04); FHIR record shows 195/194 mmHg on 2026-07-03; 120/60 mmHg on 2026-06-13.
objective.missing: Bilateral arm comparison, position (seated after 5-minute rest), and serial readings needed to characterize true baseline; 195/194 reading is clinically extreme and requires verification.

objective.vernacular: Pulse rate and whether it is regular.
Weight-to-height ratio used to estimate healthy weight range.
objective.how_obtained: Calculated from measured height and weight
objective.value: BMI 26 (patient-entered 2026-07-04); weight 185 lbs (2026-06-14); height 220 cm recorded (FHIR 2021) — height appears implausible and needs verification.
objective.missing: Verified current height needed to validate BMI; prior weight before GLP-1 therapy not documented.

objective.vernacular: Examination of the blood vessels at the back of the eye to check for damage from high blood pressure.
objective.missing: Not yet performed — essential given BP readings in the severe range.

objective.term: Serum basic metabolic panel — renal function and electrolytes
objective.vernacular: Blood test measuring kidney function (creatinine, BUN), sodium, and potassium.
objective.missing: Not yet ordered — needed to assess renal cause and end-organ damage, and to detect hypokalemia suggesting hyperaldosteronism.

objective.term: Urinalysis with microscopy — renal parenchymal screening
objective.vernacular: Urine test looking for protein, blood, or signs of kidney damage.
objective.missing: Not yet ordered.

objective.vernacular: Blood test that checks how well the thyroid gland is working.
objective.missing: Not yet ordered — patient on levothyroxine; hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism both affect blood pressure.

objective.vernacular: Blood test measuring cholesterol and triglyceride levels.
objective.missing: Not yet ordered — needed for overall cardiovascular risk stratification.

objective.vernacular: Blood tests checking blood sugar levels and average sugar control over 3 months.
objective.value: HbA1c 5.1% (2019-05-28) — within normal range at that time.
objective.missing: Current fasting glucose or repeat HbA1c needed; PCOS and prior overweight increase metabolic risk; GLP-1 use may reflect ongoing metabolic management.

objective.term: Electrocardiogram — left ventricular hypertrophy and arrhythmia
objective.vernacular: Heart tracing test to look for thickening of the heart muscle or irregular rhythms caused by high blood pressure.
objective.missing: Not yet ordered — TTE was performed 2023-06-02 (results not available); ECG still needed for current baseline.

objective.vernacular: Ultrasound of the heart to check for thickened walls or reduced pumping function.

objective.missing: Actual TTE findings (LV wall thickness, EF, diastolic function) not retrieved from record.

objective.vernacular: Blood test that checks for a hormonal cause of high blood pressure involving the adrenal glands.
objective.missing: Not yet ordered — indicated if hypokalemia found or hypertension is difficult to control.

objective.vernacular: A portable device worn for 24 hours to measure blood pressure repeatedly throughout the day and night.
objective.missing: Not yet done — highly variable readings (120/60 to 195/194) make office readings unreliable for diagnosis and treatment decisions.

objective.vernacular: A finger clip test measuring how much oxygen is in the blood.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure with no single identifiable cause — the most common type, driven by genetics, diet, lifestyle, and aging.
not_yet_testable: o-013 (ambulatory BP monitoring — not yet done)
assessment_candidates.basis: Family history of essential hypertension in first-degree relative, high sodium intake, and no clear single secondary cause identified; accounts for ~90-95% of all hypertension cases.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Most likely category but secondary causes must be actively excluded before this label is applied definitively, especially given the extreme BP reading of 195/194.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated essential hypertension causes silent, progressive damage to the heart, kidneys, brain, and eyes over years — stroke, heart attack, and kidney failure are real long-term risks.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure caused or worsened by repeated breathing pauses during sleep, which keep the nervous system activated and blood pressure high — even during the day.
not_yet_testable: o-013 (ambulatory BP monitoring — not yet done)
assessment_candidates.basis: OSA is the most prevalent secondary cause of hypertension; severe OSA diagnosed by sleep study is documented; CPAP use noted but adherence and residual AHI unknown; non-dipping nocturnal BP pattern is characteristic.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Severe OSA is confirmed — its contribution to BP elevation is highly plausible but the degree of control on CPAP is unknown.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If OSA is the main driver of hypertension and is inadequately treated, blood pressure will remain elevated despite all other interventions, maintaining high cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure made worse by regular use of anti-inflammatory pain relievers like ibuprofen, which cause the kidneys to retain salt and water.
assessment_candidates.basis: Ibuprofen appears twice in the shared care plan medication log; NSAIDs raise BP by 3–5 mmHg on average and can blunt antihypertensive therapy; frequency and dose of use not confirmed.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: Contributory role is plausible given documented ibuprofen use, but magnitude of effect depends on frequency of use, which is not yet established.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If ibuprofen is being used regularly, stopping it could meaningfully lower blood pressure — missing this means treating a reversible cause with medications instead.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure caused by an underactive or overactive thyroid gland; the patient takes thyroid replacement medication, making thyroid disease relevant.
assessment_candidates.basis: Patient is on levothyroxine (Synthroid) for known thyroid condition; both hypothyroidism (diastolic hypertension) and over-replacement causing hyperthyroidism (systolic hypertension) can elevate BP; TSH not recently documented.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: The thyroid connection is real but the direction and degree of effect depend on current TSH — this is low-effort to test and should not be left untested.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: If thyroid replacement is mis-dosed, correcting the dose may lower blood pressure without adding any new medications.

assessment_candidates.vernacular: High blood pressure caused by an adrenal gland making too much of a hormone (aldosterone) that causes salt and water retention.
assessment_candidates.basis: Accounts for up to 10% of hypertension cases and is systematically under-diagnosed; PCOS is associated with metabolic and endocrine dysregulation; hypokalemia would be a supporting clue.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: No specific symptoms pointing here, but no lab data to exclude it either — the diagnosis is missed without testing.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: Untreated primary hyperaldosteronism causes end-organ damage disproportionate to BP level and may be curable with surgery if an adrenal adenoma is found.

assessment_candidates.term: Hypertensive urgency or emergency — severe uncontrolled hypertension
assessment_candidates.vernacular: Dangerously high blood pressure (above 180/120) that is causing, or about to cause, damage to the heart, brain, kidneys, or eyes — this is a medical emergency.
not_yet_testable: o-013 (ambulatory BP monitoring — not yet done)
assessment_candidates.basis: FHIR-recorded BP of 195/194 mmHg on 2026-07-03 meets threshold for hypertensive crisis; no headache, chest pain, or visual symptoms reported, which favors urgency over emergency, but end-organ status is unconfirmed.
assessment_candidates.confidence_note: The 195/194 reading may be erroneous (diastolic nearly equal to systolic is physiologically unusual) — but it cannot be dismissed without verification; absence of symptoms does not exclude end-organ damage.
assessment_candidates.severity_vernacular: A true hypertensive emergency can cause stroke, heart failure, kidney failure, or aortic dissection within hours — if the 195/194 reading is real and unaddressed, this risk is immediate.

residual.vernacular: Something not on this list — the differential is never closed

plan_options.term: Urgent blood pressure verification and end-organ evaluation
plan_options.vernacular: Repeat blood pressure measurement (both arms, after seated rest) to confirm or refute the 195/194 mmHg reading, plus basic labs and eye exam to check for damage.
plan_options.basis: JNC8, AHA/ACC 2017 guidelines: BP ≥180/120 requires same-day evaluation to rule out hypertensive emergency before any planned elective management proceeds.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician or urgent care; patient can self-measure with validated home device as a first step.

plan_options.term: Dietary sodium restriction — DASH diet counseling
plan_options.vernacular: Reduce daily salt intake to under 2,300 mg (about 1 teaspoon) and adopt a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy — this can lower blood pressure by 5–11 mmHg.
plan_options.basis: AHA/ACC 2017 hypertension guidelines; DASH diet trials show 5–11 mmHg systolic reduction; patient already exercises most days, which is positive, but adds salt to most foods.
plan_options.who_can_act: Patient, dietitian, primary care clinician; shared decision already made to try lifestyle changes first.

plan_options.vernacular: Confirm that the CPAP machine is being used every night, download usage data, and check whether the settings are still controlling breathing pauses effectively.
plan_options.basis: Systematic reviews show consistent nightly CPAP use lowers BP by 2–3 mmHg on average; inadequate use in severe OSA may contribute more; CPAP download data is the standard of care.
plan_options.who_can_act: Sleep medicine clinician or primary care; CPAP device data downloadable by sleep lab or DME provider.

plan_options.term: Discontinuation or reduction of ibuprofen use
plan_options.vernacular: Stop or minimize ibuprofen and switch to acetaminophen for pain relief, which does not raise blood pressure.
plan_options.basis: NSAIDs are documented to raise BP 3–5 mmHg and blunt antihypertensive therapy; ACC/AHA guidelines recommend avoiding NSAIDs in hypertensive patients when alternatives exist.
plan_options.who_can_act: Patient (OTC substitution); primary care clinician (counseling and prescribing alternatives).

plan_options.term: TSH measurement to assess thyroid status on replacement therapy
plan_options.vernacular: A simple blood test to check whether the thyroid medication dose is correct — too little or too much can affect blood pressure.
plan_options.basis: Standard of care for patients on levothyroxine; target TSH 0.5–2.5 mIU/L for most adults; both under- and over-replacement affect cardiovascular parameters.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician to order; phlebotomy or lab.

plan_options.vernacular: Wearing a portable blood pressure cuff for 24 hours to get an accurate picture of blood pressure throughout the day and night, which is more reliable than a single office reading.
plan_options.basis: ACC/AHA 2017 and ESC/ESH guidelines recommend ABPM to confirm diagnosis, detect white-coat hypertension, and assess nocturnal dipping — especially relevant given highly variable readings in this record.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician to order; patient wears the device.

plan_options.term: Basic metabolic panel, urinalysis, fasting lipids, and ECG — baseline workup
plan_options.vernacular: Standard blood and urine tests plus a heart tracing to check for kidney damage, electrolyte problems, cholesterol levels, and heart thickening caused by high blood pressure.
plan_options.basis: AHA/ACC 2017 hypertension guidelines mandate baseline BMP, urinalysis, lipid panel, and ECG before or at the time of initiating any treatment strategy.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician to order; phlebotomy/lab for blood and urine; ECG technician.

plan_options.term: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio screening if hypokalemia is found
plan_options.vernacular: If the basic blood test shows low potassium, order a follow-up hormonal blood test to check whether an adrenal gland problem is causing the high blood pressure.
plan_options.basis: Endocrine Society guidelines recommend ARR screening for hypertension with hypokalemia, treatment-resistant hypertension, or onset before age 40 in a woman; PCOS adds endocrine complexity.
plan_options.who_can_act: Primary care clinician or endocrinologist to order; blood draw required under standardized conditions.
